props.title: Gossip

sections.content: Gossip sits at a fascinating intersection of late 90s/early 2000s teen thrillers like Cruel Intentions (1999) and darker explorations of truth and consequences like Gone Girl (2014). Directed by Davis Guggenheim before his pivot to documentaries, the film follows three college students who deliberately start a rumor as a social experiment, only to watch it spiral devastatingly out of control. The film captures the pre-social media era's version of viral spreading, making it both a time capsule and eerily prescient about how information - true or false - can destroy lives.

sections.content: The film's exploration of campus culture and moral ambiguity connects it to other millennial-era college dramas like The Rules of Attraction (2002) and The Skulls (2000). James Marsden, Lena Headey, and Norman Reedus play the trio of students whose "academic experiment" in rumor-spreading reveals darker truths about power, privilege, and accountability. The film's visual style, with its moody lighting and gothic architecture, creates an atmosphere of creeping dread that recalls The Craft (1996) and other supernatural-tinged teen thrillers of the era.

What makes Gossip particularly relevant today is its examination of how stories take on lives of their own once released into the wild. While the film predates social media, its insights about the viral nature of rumors and the devastating impact of false allegations feel more relevant than ever. Similar themes would later be explored in films like Easy A (2010) and Assassination Nation (2018), though with updated technology driving the narrative. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Campus Thrillers

sections.content: Gossip marks a transition point between the slick teen thrillers of the late 90s and the more psychologically complex explorations that would follow. While films like Scream (1996) and Urban Legend (1998) played with horror elements, Gossip takes a more grounded approach, examining how everyday cruelty can be just as devastating as any supernatural threat. This approach would influence later films like The Social Network (2010) and Thoroughbreds (2017), which similarly explore how privilege and power dynamics can lead to moral corruption.
